sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: brake failure versus crash-avoidance braking, blowout versus brake failure, collision priorities, crash types, and continuation details on night driving, work zones, water and crashes
Confusable pairs among emergency reactions, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A08
When conventional brakes fail you pump the pedal, but during a tire blowout you take your foot off the gas and do not brake at all. [A08]
Why it matters: group vehicle failure; confusable brake failure versus blowout.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A09
To avoid a crash with ABS you hold firm pressure without pumping, whereas with conventional brakes you pump to keep steering. [A09]
Why it matters: group crash avoidance; confusable ABS versus conventional brakes.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A07
A car floating with its windows and doors closed stays up for about three to ten minutes, while the manual separately says three to five minutes is plenty of time to get out in an emergency. [A07]
Why it matters: group water emergencies; confusable float time versus escape time.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A11
In a head-on threat with a shoulder strap and airbags you shield your face, but without a strap or airbags you throw yourself across the seat to avoid the wheel and windshield. [A11]
Why it matters: group crash types; confusable with versus without restraints.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A06
Leaving the road onto a paved shoulder is done at or near traffic speed before slowing, but drifting off the pavement by accident calls for slowing to 25 mph or less before steering back. [A06]
Why it matters: group emergency stops; confusable planned stop versus drifting off.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A01
At 70 mph on low beams at night, the table lists 154 feet of reaction distance plus 376 feet of braking distance, for 530 feet in total. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A02
Other night rules are to drive more slowly than in daylight, watch for road signs, slow or unlit vehicles, bicycles, pedestrians and animals, and keep wider safety margins. [A02]
Why it matters: group night driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A02
In heavy city traffic you need extra time to react, which means slowing down, since a lower speed buys time. [A02]
Why it matters: group city driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A03
Wide-open highways can tempt drivers to relax, but some have no signals at crossroads, so drivers must stay alert, drive defensively and keep within the speed limit. [A03]
Why it matters: group highway driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A03
In farm country or open land where livestock or deer may cross, slow down for an animal in the road until it has passed, since animals move unpredictably. [A03]
Why it matters: group road hazards; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A04
Drivers may be routed around a work zone by a detour that uses a different road, or by a diversion such as a lane shift or a crossover through the median. [A04]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A04
An End Road Work sign, or the last temporary traffic control device, marks where normal driving can resume after a work zone. [A04]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-R13 | anchor: A04
Across the nation each year, work zones see nearly 800 fatal crashes and over 37,000 serious injury crashes. [A04]
Why it matters: group work zones; dynamic statistic.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec09-R14 | anchor: A05
Through a work zone, avoid distractions such as changing radio stations or hands-free calls, watch for workers and equipment, and be patient with the crews. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; misconception hands-free is fine.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-R15 | anchor: A05
Turning the wheel sharply away from the direction of a skid can make the vehicle spin, and during a side skid you should not use the brakes. [A05]
Why it matters: group skids; misconception braking stops a skid.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-R16 | anchor: A05
Once you feel the vehicle is back under control after a skid, straighten the wheels. [A05]
Why it matters: group skids; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec09-R17 | anchor: A06
Once pulled onto the shoulder, turn on parking or emergency lights, never stand where you block the taillights at night, raise the hood, and tie a white cloth to the antenna or left door handle if you need help. [A06]
Why it matters: group emergency stops; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-R18 | anchor: A06
The short version for running off the pavement is to slow down, regain control and then turn slowly back onto the road. [A06]
Why it matters: group emergency stops; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec09-R19 | anchor: A07
Wearing a seat belt improves your odds of surviving the impact with water and is the best protection against being knocked unconscious. [A07]
Why it matters: group water emergencies; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-R20 | anchor: A07
Try power windows immediately because they may short out, and side or rear glass can only be broken with a heavy, hard object. [A07]
Why it matters: group water emergencies; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-R21 | anchor: A07
A front-engine vehicle sinks nose first, a door opens more easily once pressure inside and outside equalizes, and once outside you should follow the air bubbles to the surface. [A07]
Why it matters: group water emergencies; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec09-R22 | anchor: A08
When the engine dies, power steering fails, so grip the wheel firmly and use extra force to steer the vehicle to a safe stop off the road. [A08]
Why it matters: group vehicle failure; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-R23 | anchor: A08
If headlights suddenly go dark, stop safely off the road, try the headlight or dimmer switch, and if that fails switch on parking lights, flashers or turn signals and call for help. [A08]
Why it matters: group vehicle failure; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec09-R24 | anchor: A09
If the wipers quit during rain or snow, slow down, pull to a safe spot off the road and turn on the emergency flashers. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle failure; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-R25 | anchor: A09
When turning away from a crash, avoid braking while you turn to lessen the chance of a skid, and do not brake hard when turning onto a soft shoulder. [A09]
Why it matters: group crash avoidance; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec09-R26 | anchor: A10
Speeding up is the right choice when you are about to be struck from the side or behind and there is open room ahead, so press the gas fully, then slow once clear. [A10]
Why it matters: group crash avoidance; confusable speeding up versus stopping.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec09-R27 | anchor: A10
If a rear-end crash is coming, be ready to brake so you are not shoved into the car ahead, brace between the wheel and seat back and press your head against the headrest. [A10]
Why it matters: group crash types; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec09-R28 | anchor: A11
If you are about to be hit from the side, keep a tight grip on the wheel and be ready to turn quickly to regain control if the vehicle spins. [A11]
Why it matters: group crash types; confusable side versus rear crash.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec09-R29 | anchor: A11
After hitting a parked vehicle, you must notify the police and should also try to find the owner. [A11]
Why it matters: group after a crash; difficulty low.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec09-R30 | anchor: A11
At any crash you witness or are part of, stop, stay calm, get help from police and an ambulance, wait at the scene without blocking traffic and warn oncoming drivers. [A11]
Why it matters: group after a crash; difficulty low.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec09-R31 | anchor: A12
No written MVC crash report is needed when the police file one, and you can get a copy of their report; if shaken up, see a doctor promptly. [A12]
Why it matters: group after a crash; confusable police report versus written report.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0113]
